newsitem.title: UK: Infotech trade pact clears way for services wars.
newsitem.headline: Infotech trade pact clears way for services wars.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent

The agreement to free trade in information technology will drive European and third world countries to focus on computer services now that they have lost the hardware battle to U.S. computer giants, analysts said on Wednesday.
They said attempts by some European nations to back national computer hardware champions has now been abandoned.

Nations like India, with information technology (IT) skills which are in demand in north America, are now abandoning old theories which called for fortress economies, in favour of releasing talented citizens to sell skills to the world's computer services industry.

Later on Wednesday in Geneva, 41 nations representing 92 percent of the world's IT market are expected to sign a deal to scrap trade tariffs on computers, semiconductors, software and CD ROMS by the year 2000.

"This agreement is a triumph of common sense and realism, and it shows the centre of gravity in the IT market place has changed," said Will Cappelli, principle consultant at high-tech consultancy Ovum.

"Would-be European powerhouses like France's Bull, (Germany's) Siemens, and ICL of Britain have yielded to the Americans; the hardware battle to a large degree is over," Cappelli said. ICL is owned by Japan's Fujitsu Ltd.

"This is more seamless good news for the end user and industry, unless you truly believe in protectionism, which very few seem to these days," said Kees Dobbelaar, analyst at Gartner Group's Dataquest.

"Like oil and drinking water, IT is something you can't do without if you want to compete in the global economy, or even if you just want to have some economic growth," Keith Mallinson, managing director of Yankee Group Europe said.

Mallinson said this will complement last month's World Trade Organisation telecommunications liberalisation deal, with developing nations using Internet telephone connections to improve education and industrial management.

Ovum's Cappelli said lower tariffs will cut prices for Europeans and give them scope to raise spending closer to U.S. levels. Firms like Bull and ICL would concentrate on Internet applications like financial services and electronic commerce.
Cappelli said agreement at Geneva was possible because many developing countries have dropped old plans to develop their own indigenous hardware industries.
"India is a classic case. It is a major supplier of applications development and maintenance software services to north America and Britain," Cappelli said.

"They have a well educated workforce, but decided they can't put together the capital base to use them in hardware, but they can supply services to the developed world more cheaply. They've had an amazing success in California."

"There is a growing recognition that you can have a powerful economy without having huge industrial plant. Now the old Soviet style ideology has been dropped and they are spending money on education, not factories and concrete."
"Everybody recognises that what they used to fight about (the need for fortress economies) no longer makes sense," he said.
